opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the main thing I want with The Compendium is to give people a single place where the whole argument is laid out, start to finish, in plain language. When I talk to people, whether policymakers, journalists, or just smart people outside the AI bubble, I keep running into the same problem: they've heard fragments. "Some people think AI might be dangerous." "There's this thing called alignment." But they've never seen the full chain of reasoning: why AGI is plausible soon, why we don't know how to control it, why the race dynamics make it worse, and who is actually driving this and why.

So part of it is just explanatory. I wanted something I could hand to someone and say, "Here. Read this. This is the case, as honestly and clearly as I can make it." No hiding behind jargon, no "well, it's complicated," because a lot of it isn't that complicated. If you build systems smarter than you that you don't understand and can't control, and you're racing to do it as fast as possible, that's bad. That's not a galaxy-brained take. That's the obvious take.

The other part is that I think the discourse has been captured in a weird way. A lot of the people who talk most about AI risk are also the people building it. You get this strange situation where the labs say "this could end the world" and then raise another few billion dollars to build it faster. I wanted to name that clearly: lay out the ideologies, the incentives, the groups involved, so people can see the landscape for what it is rather than taking everyone's self-description at face value.

And ultimately the goal is action. I don't want people to read it, feel doomy, and go back to their day. I want it to be a starting point for people to say, "Okay, this is a civic problem, it's a political problem, and I'm allowed to have an opinion on it." Because I think the default path right now is bad, and the only thing that changes default paths is enough ordinary people deciding they're not okay with it.

r001.rationale: The candidate presents an argument that advanced AI may be dangerous and hard to control, but does not identify making the case that superintelligence is very likely to cause extinction as an aim of The Compendium.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the main thing I want to accomplish with The Compendium is really simple: I want there to exist, in one place, a complete, plain-language argument for why I think we are on a path toward building something smarter than us, why that's dangerous, and what I think we should actually do about it. Not a paper, not a tweet thread, not a bunch of scattered blog posts that you have to already be an insider to piece together. One document that a normal, smart, busy person can sit down with and read start to finish.

Because here's the thing. When I talk to people outside the field — policymakers, journalists, my family, whoever — the single most common experience is that they've heard bits and pieces. They've heard "AI might kill everyone," they've heard "that's science fiction," they've heard "it's just autocomplete." And they have no way of adjudicating between those claims, because nobody has ever laid out the full chain of reasoning for them. The AI safety community has, frankly, been pretty bad at this. We've spent years talking to each other in jargon and assuming the rest of the world would somehow catch up.

So The Compendium is my attempt to say: no more hiding behind jargon. Here's the argument. Here's why I think intelligence is a real thing that can be scaled. Here's why I think the people building this stuff don't actually have a plan for controlling it, and I mean that quite literally — I've asked, and the answers are not reassuring. Here's why "we'll figure it out as we go" is not a strategy when the failure mode is irreversible. And then, crucially, here's what I think we should do, because I'm tired of the framing where the only options are "race as fast as possible" or "despair."

And I want it to be falsifiable, in a sense. I want people to be able to read it and go, "okay, I disagree with step four," and then we can actually have that conversation. That's a massive improvement over where we are now, where most disagreements are really just people arguing past each other because they never agreed on what the claim even was.

The other thing — and this is maybe the part that matters most to me — is that I don't think this should be a decision made by a few hundred people in San Francisco. This is a civilizational question. Everyone has a stake in it. And you can't meaningfully participate in a decision if nobody has bothered to explain it to you. So part of the goal is just giving people the tools to have an informed opinion, whatever that opinion ends up being. If someone reads the whole thing and concludes I'm wrong, fine — at least they'll be wrong about the actual argument instead of a strawman of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says The Compendium will argue that building something smarter than humans is dangerous, but does not identify extinction as a very likely outcome.

astra-6.text: What I want to accomplish with The Compendium is to put the argument for taking AI risk seriously in one place. There are all these pieces scattered across blog posts, papers, and conversations, and it’s hard for someone coming to this fresh to understand how they fit together. I want to make the assumptions explicit: here’s what we believe, here’s why we believe it, and here’s where we’re uncertain. Then people can actually engage with the argument, find the parts they disagree with, and hopefully help us figure out what to do.

r001.rationale: The response says The Compendium aims to present an argument for taking AI risk seriously, but does not identify the specific claim that extinction from superintelligence is very likely.

sol-6.1.text: What I want to do with The Compendium is lay out how I think about AI: what we're building, why I think it could go catastrophically wrong, and what we might do about it. There's a lot of argument about individual claims, but it's hard to evaluate those without seeing the reasoning that connects them. So the goal is to put that reasoning in one place, make the assumptions explicit, and give people something they can understand, challenge, and improve.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could go catastrophically wrong, but does not identify extinction from superintelligence as very likely or say that making that case is an aim of The Compendium.
